extracted.intended_audience: industrialists, employers, philanthropists, and general readers interested in labor relations and philanthropy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles and prescriptions drawn from Andrew Carnegie's memoir on managing industrial labor relations (negotiation, strike-handling, workplace concessions) and on philanthropic distribution of great wealth (founding libraries, relief funds, research institutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor and enforce written agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: If men break an agreement there is no use in making a second agreement; employers should insist on the observance of signed agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie recounts refusing to yield when blast-furnace men threatened to leave despite an agreement that did not lapse until the end of the year; he emphasizes carrying out the provisions of an agreement one signs carelessly and resolving to be more careful next time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat worker representatives with courtesy
rubrics_metrics.description: Receive committees and workmen with genuine courtesy and respect, not merely as a policy but as a sincere practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie describes calling together committees and meeting them courteously, noting that sincere courtesy fosters good relations and that 'the more I know of working-men the higher I rate their virtues.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize ignorance as root of many disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: View the main root of trouble as ignorance, not hostility; respect workers' prejudices and 'red rags' when negotiating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing suggests education, patient explanation, and respectful handling are better conflict preventatives than confrontation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sliding-scale wages tied to product prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a wage scale that varies with the market price of the product, with a guaranteed minimum, to make capital and labor partners in prosperity and adversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie calls sliding scales the solution of the capital-labor problem; he recommends a minimum wage and that the scale last multi-year periods with notice provisions so it would likely run on for years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require clear democratic restart procedure for stopped works
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not resume operations after a shutdown until the workmen vote (Carnegie: by a two-thirds majority) to restart, ensuring collective consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He used a two-thirds restart threshold to prevent a small group from forcing resumption and to ensure legitimacy of restarting decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain individual signatures on long-term agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding multi-year scales, ask that every workman sign individually in addition to union officers' signatures to prevent union leadership alone from binding men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie allowed union officers to sign to avoid grievance, then requested each man's signature; this both removed a grievance and weakened union dues/payment compliance, making the agreement more secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be firm but avoid fighting labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers should avoid physical or bitter conflict with labor but be prepared to assert firmness and defeat improper collective actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie insists 'I will never fight you. I know better than to fight labor. I will not fight, but I can beat any committee...' — a posture of moral restraint allied with resolute leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conciliatory social engagement to defuse tensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Diffuse disputes by showing personal goodwill — e.g., entertaining workmen, showing them the city, sharing a meal — thereby changing atmosphere and building rapport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie took a committee to New York sight-seeing and lunch, deliberately avoiding discussion of the strike issue until they voted; the social approach helped secure a favorable vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit and manage internal divisions tactically
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and make use of divisions within the workers' ranks (e.g., requests to expand committees or presence of instigators) to weaken strike cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie accepted a larger committee (thirty-two) as a sign of division, and used petitioner behavior (hat incident) and meeting procedure to undercut leaders and settle disputes amicably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use procedural rebukes to discipline leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Address discourteous behavior (symbolic acts) publicly to isolate and neutralize bullies or instigators within worker delegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: asking a leader to remove his hat (a sign of discourtesy) put him on the spot and silenced him, allowing settlement without further conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide practical wage-related concessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Small administrative changes (e.g., changing pay period from monthly to every two weeks) can be as effective as wage increases for workers' standard of living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie recounts instituting biweekly pay after a worker explained the savings benefit, noting it involved a few clerks but was equivalent to a significant raise for careful men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable cooperative stores and affordable essential goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Support worker coöperatives for supplies, sell coal at net cost and arrange home delivery to reduce living expenses and indebtedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company paid rent for cooperative store premises while men took stock/manage it; coal sales at cost substantially lowered household expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide savings facilities and encourage thrift
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer to take and safeguard workers' savings (up to a cap) with interest, keeping funds separate in a trust and lending for homebuilding to encourage thrift and stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie recommended and implemented a program paying six percent interest, separate trust funds, and loans for homebuilding as an excellent aid to prudent workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstate non-violent workers; avoid punitive prosecutions
rubrics_metrics.description: After labor unrest, dismiss suits against strikers and rehire old men who did not commit violence to restore harmony and goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Homestead, Carnegie had suits dismissed and reinstated peaceful men, emphasizing reconciliation over retribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint and rely on managers who have the confidence of workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Key foremen or managers who 'like' and are liked by the men (e.g., Schwab/'Charlie') can restore order, peace, and harmony and prevent trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie credits returning an admired manager to Homestead with restoring order; personnel choices matter greatly in labor relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that appreciation and kind treatment matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Many disputes are not chiefly about wages but about lack of appreciation and kindly treatment; employers should show sincere interest in workers' welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie emphasizes that appreciation, fair dealing, and kind treatment are potent forces — doing little costs but yields big returns in loyalty and peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorten working hours as progress continues
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate progressive reduction of labor hours (Carnegie predicts eight hours will become the rule: eight for work, eight for sleep, eight for rest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an expected social advance; employers should anticipate and adapt to shorter hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cease accumulation and begin wise distribution of surplus wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: When one has amassed great wealth, resolve to stop accumulating and undertake the 'infinitely more serious' task of wise distribution for public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie describes retiring from business and using bonds and funds to create relief funds, libraries, and institutes — a personal moral imperative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize public institutions in philanthropic giving
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel major gifts to public libraries, halls, museums, technical schools and educational institutions to improve access to knowledge and opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie funded hundreds of branch libraries, a museum, picture gallery, technical schools, and the Margaret Morrison School; he saw these as returning to the communities that made his fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endow research institutions with broad liberal mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Create foundations/institutions with charters to encourage investigations, research, discovery, and application of knowledge, and to cooperate with governments and universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie's charter for the Carnegie Institution of Washington: 'To encourage in the broadest and most liberal manner investigations, research and discovery...' — stresses liberal scope and institutional cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide worker relief funds and small pensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish relief funds to assist employees suffering from accidents and to provide small pensions for the needy aged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie gave bonds to create the 'Andrew Carnegie Relief Fund' designed to relieve those who suffer from accidents and to provide small pensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anonymity or intermediaries in giving when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes give through others or anonymously so that gifts are not always accompanied by the donor's name; some benefactions should be discreet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: Carnegie (through the narrator) gave money secretly to McLuckie; later publicity sometimes obscured the original purpose, showing both the value and pitfalls of anonymous giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select distinguished and cooperative governance for foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: When founding large institutions, appoint respected, capable directors and consult public leaders to ensure credibility and effective governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie consulted President Roosevelt and enlisted distinguished figures (e.g., D.C. Gilman, Elihu Root) as directors for the Carnegie Institution; Roosevelt praised the chosen board as irreplaceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give during lifetime to guide proper use
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribute wealth while alive to supervise and guide its application toward beneficial public ends rather than leaving it unguided by bequests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie framed distribution as a serious task of old age after retiring, choosing active endowment of institutions and funds rather than passive accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philanthropy should aim to 'undo excess' and secure sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral purpose of distribution is to undo excess wealth so 'each man have enough' — philanthropic gifts should aim to secure basic sufficiency and uplift society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He quotes Shakespeare and frames his philanthropic mission as ensuring that excess is redistributed so everyone has enough; this provides an ethical framing for types of gifts made.
